title: A Day of Very Low Probability

tiles.alt: A moonlit night sky. A single hair-thin silver thread catches the light. / Beneath the moonlight glints a tiny fragment of silver, a fraction of a line…
Black robes tumble through the moonlit air like crows. / (black robes, falling)
Darkness. A red stain rising. A scream too loud to read. / …blood spills out in litres, and someone screams a word.
Title: Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality. Chapter One: A Day of Very Low Probability. / Harry Potter / and the / Methods of Rationality / CHAPTER ONE · A Day of Very Low Probability
A row of Victorian brick houses in the rain. One window glows warm. / Oxford, England. The wettest July anyone could remember.

A cosy living room drowning in books: shelves to the ceiling, heaps under the window. A man and a woman stand arguing by the fire. A small boy with messy black hair and round glasses reads in an armchair. / Every inch of wall space is covered by a bookcase. / And it still isn't enough. / This is the home of Professor Michael Verres-Evans, his wife Petunia Evans-Verres, and their adopted son, Harry James Potter-Evans-Verres.
Close on the coffee table: a parchment envelope addressed in emerald ink to Mr H. Potter. / There is a letter on the table. Yellowish parchment. Emerald ink. No stamp.
Dad: You're joking. / Mum: My sister was a witch. / Mum: Her husband was a wizard.
Dad: This is absurd! They were at our wedding! They came for Christmas!
Mum: I told them you weren't to know.
Harry peers over the top of a large book, eyes darting between his parents. / …
Dad: Dear, I understand you're not familiar with the sceptical literature. / Dad: A trained magician can fake almost anything. Remember how I taught Harry to bend spoons?
Mum: It wasn't bending spoons— / Mum: Michael. I wasn't… always like this.

Memory, in sepia: two teenage sisters. The red-haired one makes flowers bloom in her palm. The plainer one watches, arms crossed. / “Lily was always the pretty one. And then she got magic. Can you imagine how I felt?”
“I begged her to use it on me. For years. She always said no—the most ridiculous excuses. A centaur told her not to…”
“Then I started going out with a boy called Vernon Dursley. He said he wanted a son, and he'd name him Dudley.” / Vernon: Dudley Dursley. Good strong name, that. / Petunia: Dudley… Dursley?
“So she gave in. I drank a potion. I was sick for weeks… and when I got better, I was beautiful.”
Mum: After that I couldn't hate her any more. Especially when I learned what her magic brought her in the end.
Dad: Darling. You got sick, you rested in bed, and your skin cleared up on its own. / Mum: She was a witch. I saw it.
Dad: Petunia. You know that can't be true. Do I really have to explain why?
Mum: My love, I know I can't win arguments with you, but please, just this once—
Harry leaps up on the armchair, fists clenched, book flying. / Harry: DAD! MUM!
They looked at him as though they'd forgotten there was a third person in the room.
Harry: Mum, your parents didn't have magic, did they? / Harry: So when Lily got her letter… how did they get convinced?
Mum: Ah… They didn't just send a letter. They sent a professor from Hogwarts. / Mum: She showed us some magic.

Harry, lit up with the idea, spreads his hands. / Harry: Then you don't have to fight about this! / Harry: We get a Hogwarts professor here, and we look. If it's real, Dad admits it. If it isn't, Mum admits it. / Harry: That's what experiments are for! So we don't have to settle things by arguing!
Dad: Oh, come now, Harry. Really—magic? / Dad: I thought you'd know better than to take this seriously, son. Even if you're only ten.
Harry was given anything reasonable he wanted. Books. Tutors. Every maths competition he cared to enter. / Anything, except the slightest shred of respect.
Extreme close-up on Harry's eyes, gone flat and cold. Frost creeps at the edges of the panel. / Harry: Sometimes Harry wanted to scream at his father.
Mum: —just once, trust your wife who loves you— / Dad: —it isn't a question of trust, dear, it's a question of evidence— / Harry: I'm going to go to my room.
Harry climbs the staircase alone; muffled argument drifts up from below. / Mum: —never listen— / Dad: —being hysterical— / And they went on fighting while Harry climbed the stairs.
Harry: The funny thing is, I should agree with Dad.
Harry: No-one has ever seen real evidence of magic. It should be a clean case for Mum joking, lying, or being insane… / Harry: …in ascending order of awfulness.
The Hogwarts envelope in the candlelight. / Harry: Except some part of me is utterly certain that magic is real. / Harry: Where do you come from, strange little prediction?
Harry: Well. The thing to do with a testable hypothesis— / Harry: —is to go and test it.
This called for careful calligraphy.
Harry's letter to Hogwarts, in careful handwriting. / P.S. — My father is highly sceptical. I myself am uncertain.
Red wax drips onto the envelope flap; Harry has pressed his initials into it with a penknife: H.J.P.E.V. / If he was going to descend into this madness, he was going to do it with style.
His father was reading a book of higher maths, to show how smart he was. / His mother was cooking his father's favourite dinner, to show how loving she was.
As scary as arguments could be, not arguing was somehow much worse.
Harry: Mum, I'm going to test the hypothesis. According to your theory, how do I send an owl to Hogwarts? / Mum: I—I don't know. I think you just have to own a magic owl?
Harry: Well, the letter got here somehow. I'll wave it around outside and ask for an owl. / Harry: Dad, do you want to come and watch?
His father shook his head, minutely, and kept on reading.
Harry: Of course.

The back garden at dusk after rain. Harry stands alone on the wet lawn holding the envelope. / Standing in your own back garden, about to shout for an owl, it occurs to you that this is… actually pretty embarrassing.
Harry: No. I'm better than Dad. / Harry: I will use the scientific method even if it makes me feel stupid.
Harry: Letter—
Low angle: Harry thrusts the envelope at the enormous evening sky and yells. / Harry: LETTER FOR HOGWARTS! CAN I GET AN OWL?
?: Harry?
Harry whipped his arm down and hid the envelope behind his back like it was drug money.
An old woman in a hairnet peers over the fence, a grey cat perched beside her. / Mrs Figg: What are you doing, Harry? / Harry: Nothing! Just—testing a really silly theory—
Mrs Figg: Did you get your acceptance letter from Hogwarts?
Harry, frozen.

Harry: …Yes. I got a letter from Hogwarts. They want my owl by the 31st of July, but— / Mrs Figg: But you don't have an owl! Poor dear. I can't imagine what someone was thinking, sending you just the standard letter.
A wrinkled hand reaches over the fence; Harry hands up the envelope. / Hardly thinking at all by now, Harry handed it over.
Mrs Figg: Just leave it to me, dear. In a jiffy or two I'll have someone over.
The old woman has gone. Her grey cat stays on the fence, looking straight at Harry. / And her face disappeared from over the fence. / The cat stayed.
A wide, quiet shot: Harry alone on the lawn under a huge evening sky with a single first star. / There was a long silence in the garden.
Harry: What.
To be continued / Next: Everything I Believe Is False
